articles.title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
articles.summary: The president named his national intelligence chief as the taskforce's head as worries over AI grow.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.

Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.
The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.

Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.
"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.
The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.
Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump.

articles.title: PNP requires gun vault photo for new, renewed firearm licenses
articles.summary: After school shootings, PNP adds gun storage proof to license applications.

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 11:37am
Sport gun enthusiasts undergo firearms training under the guidance of range officers at the ARMSCOR firing range in Marikina City on June 27, 2026
The STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — Private individuals applying for or renewing a license to own and possess firearms must now submit a photo showing their firearm storage facility as part of tighter gun safekeeping requirements taking effect Monday, October 5.

In an October 1 advisory, the Philippine National Police's Firearms and Explosives Office said applicants must declare that proper storage and safety measures are available for their firearms before their License to Own and Possess Firearms application can be approved.
The FEO has revised its application forms for both new and renewing license holders to reflect the requirement.

"Please be informed that effective October 5, 2026, the Firearms and Explosives Office Form No. 1 (Revision - September 2026) and Firearms and Explosives Office Form No. 2 (Revision - September 2026) application forms shall be used for all new and renewal LTOPF transactions," the advisory read.
Applicants must submit a photo of themselves with their firearm vault or storage container, which must be secured by a lock and key, along with the other documentary requirements.

The requirement to safely store firearms itself is not new. Existing firearms regulations already require holders of Type 1 to Type 5 licenses to keep their guns in a vault or container secured by lock and key or other appropriate security measures.
The new FEO policy, however, adds documentary proof of compliance to the application process.
Stricter safekeeping
The stricter requirement comes after a series of fatal school shootings this year linked to minors' use of firearms licensed to adults.

In the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, one of the two minor suspects used a Glock pistol issued to his aunt, a police officer. The officer later told a Senate inquiry that the gun had been kept in a locked plastic locker rather than a safety vault.

In August, a student who carried out a shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University used two firearms belonging to his father, a Customs police officer. The Bureau of Customs confirmed that one was agency-issued while the other was his licensed personal firearm.

A third school shooting in Banga, South Cotabato, on September 18 involved a licensed firearm owned by the shooter's father, a Department of Education employee. Authorities said the firearm had been kept in a vault that the student was able to open or break into.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla had earlier proposed allowing police to inspect the homes of licensed gun owners to verify proper storage, arguing that firearm ownership in the Philippines is a privilege that carries responsibilities. He later clarified that the proposed inspections would require gun owners to consent through a waiver and receive prior notice.
The PNP has also said it would tighten firearms safekeeping rules for police personnel following the school shooting incidents.

articles.title: 'Missed opportunity': Law prof faults prosecution's Sara property presentation
articles.summary: He says documents should support its explanation of the questioned Samal property.

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 10:11am

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors missed a chance to clearly establish whether properties registered to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband were omitted from her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, a law professor said.

Adonis Gabriel, a professor at the San Beda University College of Law, said prosecutors should have presented the couple's relevant property titles together and compared them with Duterte's declared assets.

"With all due respect to the prosecution, nagkulang ang prosecution sa paglalahad nila ng testimonya ng mga tao natin sa [Land Registration Authority]," Gabriel said in Filipino in an interview with dzBB on October 2.
(With all due respect to the prosecution, it fell short in presenting the testimony of the Land Registration Authority personnel.)

In particular, Gabriel referred to the October 1 testimony of the registers of deeds of Davao City and Samal under Article II of Duterte's impeachment case, which mainly accuses her of unexplained wealth and failure to divest from business interests.

The witnesses identified land titles, deeds of sale and tax declarations for properties registered to Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. Both repeatedly said they could not determine whether the properties matched entries in Duterte's SALNs.

Gabriel said prosecutors should have presented all relevant titles and compared them with the properties declared in Duterte's SALNs. Any registered property left unmatched, he said, could then have been clearly identified as potentially undeclared.
"Ang ginawa ng prosecution, inilahad lamang nila ang isang titulo ng isang property," Gabriel said. (What they just did was to state the title of one property.)

He noted that SALNs do not require property title numbers, making a direct comparison based on the title number alone impossible. The form instead requires identifying details such as the property's location and type, assessed and fair market values, acquisition year and mode, and acquisition cost.

"Sa paglalahad ng mga testigo sa korte, para ka ring naglalahad ng kuwento sa ating mga hukom. Sa paglalahad ng kuwento, dapat maipakita mo nang malinaw iyong gusto mong impormasyon na lumabas," Gabriel said. (Presenting witnesses in court is like telling a story to the judges. You must clearly show the information you want to establish.)
Gabriel said the prosecution fell short because it did not make that comparison sufficiently clear.
"So that's a missed opportunity for the prosecution dahil hindi nila nailahad nang malinaw na may mga properties doon sa SALN ng ating bise presidente na hindi naisama," he said.
(So that's a missed opportunity for the prosecution because they were not able to clearly establish that there were properties not included in the vice president's SALN.)
Undisclosed documents
Gabriel said Duterte's camp also needed to substantiate its explanation for a questioned property in Samal.

The defense said during cross-examination that a property appeared in Duterte's 2013 SALN, while the property questioned by prosecutors was transferred to her in 2018. The defense's theory, Gabriel said, was that the property had been acquired through a contract to sell beginning in 2013, with ownership formally transferred in 2018.
Gabriel said the defense should produce the contract to sell, payment records, tax documents and records of improvements to establish that the earlier SALN entry referred to the same property.
"Kaya ang inaasahan ko sa ating bise presidente bilang public officer, kailangan niya ring patunayan na iyong property na hinahanap ninyo ay ito iyong nakarehistro noong 2013," Gabriel said.
(What I expect of the vice president as a public officer is that she also substantiate that the property being questioned is the one recorded in 2013.)
Gabriel said a general denial would not be enough and stressed the transparency expected of public officials.
"Bilang public officer, kailangan maging transparent tayo. Iyan ang purpose ng statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth," he said.
(As public officers, we need to be transparent. That is the purpose of the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.)

After presenting records on real properties and firearms last week, prosecutors are moving into Duterte and Carpio's financial records on Monday, October 5. Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura has been called to testify as the prosecution seeks to compare financial transactions with the couple's declared assets and net worth.

articles.title: Jane Doe at centre of Cornell rape case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
articles.summary: The woman who has alleged she was drugged and raped by ‌Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.

image.caption: Students walk past the entrance of Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Thursday. (Lauren Petracca/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
The woman who has alleged she was drugged and raped by ‌Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.
Cornell under scrutiny following outcry over university's handling of allegations

Thomas Giuffra, who represents the woman identified as Jane Doe, told CNN that people have threatened to silence or harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity drugged and ​raped her in 2024.
"She's received multiple threats," Giuffra said on CNN's State ​of the Union, adding that he had also been threatened.

"I'm not afraid of these people," he said. "But the threats, the abuse to protect what's going on, the status quo — these guys are ​disgusting. They should stay in their mother's basement and stay out of the world."

The identity of ⁠Jane Doe has become ⁠part of the fevered online conversation surrounding the case. Women ‌on social media have been posting #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with the accuser and to counter some who have sought to publicly name her.
Advocate calls for 'overhaul' of student groups to address harms on campuses like Cornell

Michael Tracey, an independent journalist and commentator, posted on Friday what he said was the accuser's name, which Reuters was unable to verify, before quickly deleting it, saying his point had been ⁠made.

He has expressed sympathy for the accused men over what he says is the harassment they have faced and described his effort to name the Cornell accuser as journalistic diligence protected under the U.S. Constitution as free speech.

items: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
'I am Jane Doe': Online rally to protect Cornell rape accuser's identity becomes a reckoning

blocks.text: He told Reuters on Sunday ‌that he did not wish to encourage threats or harassment against the woman.

"The point, from my perspective, was more about the public-policy implications of this increasingly commonly used tactic in civil litigation, for plaintiffs' attorneys to introduce sensational, reputation-harming allegations using the cloak of anonymity for their clients," Tracey said in an interview.
N.Y. governor appoints special prosecutor to Cornell sexual assault case

Cornell University president ​Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message on Saturday that the university will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus following the outcry over the ⁠school's handling of the rape allegations.

"At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a ⁠powerful sense of community," he said. "But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility."
Since the lawsuit was ⁠filed last ⁠month, prosecutors in New York's Tompkins County have ​been criticized for their initial handling of the allegations in 2024.

items: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency

blocks.text: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney ​General Letitia James as special prosecutor ⁠to look into the case.

U.S. President Donald Trump, a critic of James for years, lambasted the decision to appoint her. "And I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake," he told reporters on Friday.
Asked about Trump's comment, Giuffra said the case shouldn't be politicized. "It has nothing to do with politics," he said.

articles.title: US pulls bombers out of UK's Fairford airbase after arrests
articles.summary: Following a suspected terrorist plot targeting the UK's Fairford airbase, the US Air Force withdrew all its B-1 planes from the site.

image.caption: US B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford were used for strikes against IranImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A week after several men were detained at the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in the UK's Fairford on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks, a Pentagon official announced that the United States had removed its B-1 bombers from the base northwest of London.
On Sunday, aircraft monitoring sites showed the B-1 aircraft flying out of the UK base.

"While operational security precluded us from ​confirming the movement of our assets and forces ​in real-time, ‌we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home ‌stations in the United States," a Pentagon spokesman wrote ‌in ​a statement.

A dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the British airbase used by the US. London previously allowed the Pentagon to fly sorties out of Fairford against Iranian missile sites which were threatening ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What do we know about the suspected plot
Last Sunday, police were called to a base in southwest England after a local farmer reported a group of men in several vans engaging in "suspicious" activity.

Investigators blocked off the area and called in the bomb disposal teams. However, no explosives were found in the vehicles. Later, the five British nationals arrested in connection to the incident were released on bail.
US President Donald Trump voiced his disappointment over their release.
On Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that Britain had "strong indications" that Iran was involved in a suspected plot targeting the base.
Iran dismissed the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran to discuss the issue.

articles.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
articles.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.

blocks.text: Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.

Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.

The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.

Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.

"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.

"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.

On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.

Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.

"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.

A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.

"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.

India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.

"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."

More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.

"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

articles.title: Former Bachelor star Sam Wood charged with domestic violence
articles.summary: Fitness influencer, 46, faces court on Monday after his arrest in Noosa at the weekend The fitness influencer and reality TV star Sam Wood has been charged in Queensland with domestic violence…

blocks.text: The fitness influencer and reality TV star Sam Wood has been charged in Queensland with domestic violence offences.
The personal trainer and star of the third season of reality TV show The Bachelor was charged on Sunday and spent the weekend in police custody after an alleged incident on Saturday night.

Mark Watkin, acting CEO of 28 Group, now the parent company of fitness business 28 by Sam Wood, said in a statement on Monday that the company was “shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood.”
“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties,” Watkin said.
“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”

A statement posted simultaneously to Wood’s personal Instagram account and that of his wife, Snezana Wood, on Monday morning, said: “This is a difficult time for all of us, we are working through this as a family and are thoroughly co-operating with authorities.”
On Sunday, Queensland police confirmed they had arrested a 46-year-old Victorian man and charged him with domestic violence offences.
The arrest came after officers attended a Noosa address about 9pm on Saturday night after receiving reports of alleged domestic violence.
The man has been charged with assaulting occasioning bodily harm (domestic violence) and strangulation in a domestic setting, police said.
The alleged victim or victims have not been identified.
Wood was refused bail and was expected to appear in Maroochydore magistrates court on Monday.
The personal trainer shot to national prominence when he starred as the eponymous Bachelor in the third season of the reality TV show franchise in 2015.
He met Snezana Markoski when she was a contestant on the show. The couple married in 2018 in Byron Bay. They have four daughters including one from Markoski’s previous relationship.
Wood owns and runs personal training studio The Woodshed in Brighton East, Melbourne.
He built a fitness and nutrition business, 28 by Sam Wood, off the back of his increased profile from The Bachelor, eventually selling the company in 2022 for $71.2m.

Over the past year, the Australian Taxation Office has been pursuing Wood for alleged unpaid tax debts, reported to be in excess of $7 million. Case listings noted in August that a settlement had been reached, with the case dismissed in September.
Wood has recently launched a telehealth-based weight-loss platform aimed at middle-aged women, called Ollo for Women.
Guardian Australia has approached businesses connected to Wood for comment.

articles.title: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government launches military drive to retake all Houthi-held territory
articles.summary:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new…

blocks.text: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”

The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.

Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.

Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.

Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: World·New

Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil's veteran president, will face off on Oct. 25 in a run-off for the top job of Latin America's powerhouse economy.
Run-off between incumbent and son of previous president to be held Oct. 25

The country's electoral court in Brasília said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro will reach 50 per cent or more of the total vote needed for a first-round win.
The run-off election will be held on Oct. 25. The next presidential term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

articles.title: Brazil’s presidential race to go to second round as Flávio Bolsonaro leads incumbent Lula
articles.summary:
Far-right challenger and son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro will now face leftwing president in runoff vote

Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.

With more than 98% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47.3%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 44.8%.

Bolsonaro will go into the second round as favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.2%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.

Brazil’s far-right put in a stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.

On Sunday morning, as Lula cast his vote in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial hub in the São Paulo metropolitan area where he began his political career more than half a century ago, the former union leader said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice.

“People are going to have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism,” Lula told reporters, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld, including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro urged Brazilians to end Lula’s ‘era of backwardness’.  Photograph: Mateus Bonomi/Reuters

blocks.text: After voting in Rio, where the Bolsonaro political dynasty was born in the late 80s, Flávio Bolsonaro urged Brazilians to end what he called Lula’s “era of backwardness”. “I’m more than ready to lead this country and to give Brazilian families the right to dream once again,” claimed Bolsonaro, who has promised an iron-fisted crackdown on crime, despite his ties to members of Rio’s paramilitary mafias.

Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.

Allies of the veteran leftwinger call the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
“Brazilian democracy is at stake,” said Talíria Petrone, a leftwing congresswoman from Rio who is seeking reelection.

Speaking at Lula’s final pre-vote rally in Rio, Petrone called for tactical voting to prevent the Bolsonaro clan returning to power. “I’m sure that even those people who don’t like Lula know that Flávio Bolsonaro must be defeated – and the only way is a fourth presidential term for president Lula,” Petrone said.

Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo, but want to vote Lula out of power.
As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters are choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate.

Speaking on the eve of the election, Maria Tereza Fazzio, 74, a retired psychologist from Rio, said she had voted for Lula ever since he first ran for the presidency in 1989 – four years after the end of Brazil’s 21-year dictatorship. She vowed to do so again this year, in order to protect social programmes implemented by Lula and out of fear that a Bolsonaro victory could put her country’s democracy in jeopardy.
“All he talks about is granting an amnesty to his dad and all the others who are in prison [because of the 2022-23 coup attempt] – he hasn’t got any policy agenda,” she said of Bolsonaro.

blocks.caption: A Lula supporter dressed as Our Lady of Aparecida at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday. A row over the saint has caused a nationwide outcry – which could favour Lula, who is Catholic.  Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters

blocks.text: Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.

However, his momentum appeared to have been interrupted by a row involving Brazil’s Catholic patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida. Speculation that Bolsonaro – who is part of Brazil’s fast-growing evangelical community – might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic.

On Sunday, an influential Catholic bishops’ organisation, the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, posted a thinly veiled swipe at Bolsonaro on social media. “May God grant us wisdom and courage to build together a reconciled, sovereign, just, and fraternal Brazil,” the group wrote on X, calling on Our Lady of Aparecida to protect the country.

Donald Trump also became a key election issue, with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

articles.title: Brazil election: Bolsonaro and Lula head to runoff
articles.summary: Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral…

image.caption: The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da SilvaImage: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS

blocks.text: With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.
With nearly 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote. Lula has 45%, according to the electoral court.
Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff.
Bolsonaro is monitoring the vote count in Brasilia, the country's capital, while Lula is following it from Sao Paulo.
Because Brazil uses electronic voting machines, final results are expected to be available within several hours of the polls closing.
You can watch our livestream on the Brazil election results below.
Right gains momentum in Brazil

Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil, making it difficult for Lula to change the course of the election.
"He still has a chance, based on the numbers, but the momentum is with the right," said de Sa e Silva.
"The big news tomorrow will be not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said.
He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term.
Lula vows to 'defeat the far right'
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

blocks.caption: Long queues of voters were seen in parts of Rio de JaneiroImage: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right."
Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.

blocks.caption: The 80-year-old Lula is seeking the presidency for a fourth and final timeImage: Amanda Perobelli/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bolsonaro calls for 'change'

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro has said he would pardon his father if electedImage: Douglas Shineidr/AFP

blocks.text: The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

blocks.caption: US President Trump had held close ties with fellow right-wing populist Jair Bolsonaro [FILE March 2019]Image: Chris Kleponis/CNP/MediaPunch/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.
In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.
Brazil election: Lula, Bolsonaro focus on women's vote

articles.title: White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt
articles.summary:
Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says

The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a…

blocks.text: The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.

Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.

According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.

In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.

The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.
A screenshot of that post, published by the Daily Mirror, shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.”
Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it was shared on social media by an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which also identified her as an aide to Gosar.

The next day, Harmony replied to the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”, Harmony replied with a one-word answer: “Uncle.”
Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspired a viral meme featuring a variation of the slogan.

Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist.

“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!”

Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him.

Trump has tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him.

Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement.

Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glenn pointedly asked Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter.

During a press availability on Air Force One last month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trump a series of friendly questions that seemed designed to help him score political points. As TMZ reported on Friday, Associated Press photographs taken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions.

Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after delivering an on-air tribute to the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor.

The station’s news director denied that Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.

articles.title: Serb nationalist credits Trump, Putin after declaring his party's victory in Bosnian election
articles.summary: Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia on Sunday that was shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation…

image.caption: People cast ballots at a polling station in Sarajevo, Bosnia, on Sunday. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia on Sunday that was shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war.
Milorad Dodik was barred from office, but his separatist rhetoric dominated campaign

Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that has sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia.

Formerly the president of the country's Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war.

With nearly 90 per cent of votes counted, Dodik's ally, Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, had more than 55 per cent of votes to take one of the three seats in the country's tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by about 30 percentage points.

Speaking at a news conference late Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a "vast majority" in Republika Srpska's assembly, and he credited U.S. President Donald Trump's "magnificent victory" in 2024 and Russian President Vladimir Putin's support for the election win.
"No one should ask us to change our politics," Dodik said. "We will not give up, but continue for our people.... I cannot believe that we smashed it like this."

About 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country's multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.

items: Ratko Mladic, war criminal and former Bosnian Serb military leader, dead

blocks.text: With more than 94 per cent of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegovic, by fewer than three percentage points.
Both Filipovic and Becirovic declared victory in their races late Sunday before all votes were counted.
Bosnia's Central Election Commission said that a total of 1,432,269 votes were cast, a turnout of 42 per cent — down by about eight per cent from Bosnia's last election in 2022.

Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a U.S.-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.
Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia's national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country.
At his party's final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska's administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia "is dead."
"It is an impossible country. It doesn't make any sense," he said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian Ambassador Igor Kalabukhov.

items: Genocide denial leave Bosniaks stuck in a violent past

blocks.text: Such political and ethnic divisions — in which the country's Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines — have blocked Bosnia's progress toward joining the EU, despite the bloc's efforts to encourage the country's divided leaders to work together for reform.

Dragan Bursac, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he "is still in command. He is everywhere.... It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them."
Ethnic tensions simmer

One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades after the war that started in 1992, after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.

Bosnia's wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladic, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.
Bosnian Serbs view Mladic as a hero despite his conviction by a United Nations court over the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995, and other atrocities.
New electronic election security

Sunday's election was the first time Bosnia used electronic identification of voters and ballot scanners to prevent irregularities or organized voter manipulation, which have cast doubt on the fairness of previous elections.

On Sunday morning, Associated Press journalists reported seeing multiple polling places where voting couldn't begin on time because of difficulties with the new digital technology. Bosnia's election commission announced late Sunday that some polling stations that had experienced disruptions earlier in the day would be permitted to remain open past the 7 p.m. cut-off time.

On Sunday, some voters in Banja Luka expressed concern that the new digital systems could confuse older voters. Republika Srpska's Interior Ministry said in a statement that of 1,957 polling stations in the entity, there had been delays at 201.

articles.title: Kids and young adults are addicted to screens. New research argues it may be a public health concern

image.caption: The physical and mental well-being of millions of kids around the world may be at risk because of excess screen time, according to global data analyzed for a new series of research papers published Sunday by the medical journal The Lancet. (Jc Milhet/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Andrea Chrysanthou says it's been almost impossible to limit her 13-year-old son Nathaniel's screen time.

"My son understands that he's addicted," said Chrysanthou, the Toronto-based board chair of the advocacy group Children First Canada. She says he's asked her for help to stop using his digital device so much, but the minute she turns her back, he's reaching for it again.

Her son is like millions of other kids around the world whose physical and mental well-being are at risk because of excess screen time, according to a new series of research papers published Sunday by medical journal The Lancet.

It's a broad review of international studies that allowed researchers to distill the potential harms and benefits of digital technology, and offers a sense of "what needs to happen to protect children's health," said co-author Jay Shaw, an assistant professor in the University of Toronto's Department of Physical Therapy.

Despite the breadth of their analysis, Shaw and his colleagues say the true severity of the issue can't be fully understood or addressed without access to tech companies' own user data — something those companies are currently under no obligation to share.
But they say their research makes the case that screen addiction among young people is a public health issue that requires governments to intervene.
Parents can't be the only line of defence, Chrysanthou told CBC News.
"We want the companies and the platforms to take responsibility, to make their platforms safe."
LISTEN | How do we determine the quality of screen time at school:
The Current23:13Has screen time at school gone too far?
A 'clear' picture
Shaw and his fellow researchers reviewed data from 2,790 studies comprised of more than nine million participants.
Among the youngest users of digital devices, age 10 and under, too much screen time was linked to sleeping less and affected cognitive, emotional and social development.
There was a wider range of implications for young people between the ages of 10 and 24, from mental health problems and reduced physical activity to substance abuse, self-harm and suicidal ideation.
"I think we're in a moment globally right now, where the harms associated with digital media use, especially for young people, have become quite clear," Shaw told CBC News.

items: Canada is the latest to try limiting kids' social media exposure — but new bill gives platforms room to change
'I'd cry my eyes out': Some P.E.I. teens push back on proposed social media restrictions

blocks.text: Dr. Rachel Mitchell, a psychiatrist at Toronto's Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, says this research confirms that tech and social media companies need to share responsibility.

She says most digital platforms and applications weren't designed for young people, noting that kids five and under and adolescents are at a time in their lives when their brains are still developing and they are more vulnerable.

Mitchell says they're being bombarded with digital distractions from various applications, games and platforms that often aim to capture constant attention by employing features like autoplay, push notifications and elements of gamification, along with daily rewards for online activity.
"Adults, at least, have fully developed frontal lobes with which to regulate, and they can't even do it themselves," she said, referring to the ability to limit screen use.
"So, why we're expecting children to do it is beyond me."
Experts blame AI, screens for slipping Canadian student test scores
Tech's 'big tobacco' moment?

Shaw says there's a long history of public health interventions when it comes to health-related concerns about certain habits, such as smoking. He says the addictive nature of social media and other digital platforms should be no different.
And society, he says, may be at its "so-called big tobacco moment" with technology.
"If we don't get out in front of it, then digital technologies will end up being more harmful than beneficial for public health."
But Mitchell says addressing excess screen use, especially for young people, is a different scenario than smoking.
She says there are no real benefits to smoking, while digital devices and media serve many purposes in our daily lives.
A cigarette, she adds, won't help you find your way around the city — but a phone will.

In fact, Mitchell points out, the data review in The Lancet highlights the positive benefits of digital media for young people when it's used in moderation, as well as when it's used for education and extracurricular learning.
But, she says in order to leverage the benefits, the risks of these technologies need to be managed.

Mitchell says this new research series demonstrates that the risks are so high and affect such a wide population that it's no longer ethically or morally possible for people to manage without intervention from the government or the tech companies themselves.
Some social media and tech companies have implemented tools aimed at helping parents reduce the amount of time their children spend scrolling.

Meta, the parent company of social media platforms Facebook and Instagram, agreed to implement age limits in the U.S. when it settled a multi-state class-action lawsuit for $18 billion US in August. It was described as the largest state consumer protection settlement in history outside of the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.

items: Screen time can affect children's language development, study suggests
Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools

blocks.text: TikTok has a default setting that limits usage to one hour for users between the ages of 13 to 17, but this setting can be changed or turned off.
The head of Snapchat's parent company, Snap Inc., recently told BBC News the company is open to time restrictions for teens.
Steps like these, Mitchell says, are "absolutely necessary" and "should have been there from day one."
Parents, experts warm on proposed social media ban but want details
Push for tech company transparency
Shaw and his fellow researchers hope the review can help governments shape public health policy to address the potential harms that the overuse of digital media has on young people.

But he says without access to user data from big tech companies, it will be difficult to get a true picture of how much young people are interacting with digital devices and of the true toll it takes on their physical and mental well-being.
Their series of papers notes that tech giants like Meta, TikTok and Google aren't obligated to share such data or details about how their algorithms fuel prolonged use, especially among young people.
"It's very hard to reconcile morally, ethically, how that data cannot be available to researchers," Mitchell said.

Digital safety legislation like the federal government's proposed Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34) would, if passed, compel tech platforms to be transparent and provide accredited researchers with access to electronic data related to online safety.
Bill C-34 would also force social media companies to restrict accounts for children under 16 unless the platforms can implement adequate safeguards to protect them.

items: Ottawa moves to restrict social media for kids under 16
Q&A: This doctor says he's seeing the harms of social media on youth

blocks.text: The bill, which has yet to be debated in the House of Commons, has drawn criticism over whether it may violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
But neither Mitchell nor Shaw and his colleagues are making the case to ban children from using social media — even Children First Canada's Chrysanthou isn't sure it would work.

She says that in places like Australia, where age limits on social media were put in place earlier this year, many kids remain online, having found a way around restrictions or because the tech companies haven't employed effective checks.
"Beyond some kind of regulations around screen time," Chrysanthou said, "we want the companies and the platforms to take responsibility, to make their platforms safe."
Parents push back against screen time in schools

articles.title: Forced to call him 'Dad': Trial over sexual abuse in disabled care home shocks South Korea
articles.summary: The BBC spoke to one of three residents at a care home who were sexually assaulted by a staff member.

blocks.text: Forced to call him 'Dad': Trial over sexual abuse in disabled care home shocks South Korea
Image source, Getty Images
"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."
These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.

She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.
Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.
The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.
The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.
We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.
'I just endured it'
Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.
The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.

Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.

As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The care home was located in the Korean city of Incheon

blocks.text: The care home was located in the Korean city of Incheon
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.

For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.

In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.

According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Saekdongwon was asked to close down in light of this case

blocks.text: Image source, SADD TV
Saekdongwon was asked to close down in light of this case
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.

"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.

Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."

The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".
Public scrutiny and protests

The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.

That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.

These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.
But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.
A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.
The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some residents had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating

blocks.text: Some residents had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating

Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.
Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.

One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.

Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.
And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.
In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.
In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.

"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."
'We want to live in peace'

Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".

In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.
The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.
Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.
Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."
She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted.
What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".
But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe.
"I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

articles.title: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby promises new tax on millionaires to pay for health care
articles.summary: British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says his party will introduce a new tax bracket for those who earn $1 million or more to help pay for health care, if re-elected.

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby made a stop in Comox, B.C., to speak with voters on Oct. 4, 2026. (CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says his party will introduce a new tax bracket for those who earn $1 million or more to help pay for health care, if re-elected.
The top two tax brackets would see a rate hike in addition to a new tax bracket
B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is promising to tax people earning $1 million or more at a rate of 24.5 per cent if re-elected, with the revenue to help fund health care.
In a Sunday press release, the B.C. NDP said that only the top two tax brackets would see rates rise by two percentage points, while brackets below that would go unchanged.
Right now, those who make $1 million or more a year are taxed at a rate of 20.5 per cent, the highest tax bracket in B.C.
But the new $1-million income tax bracket Eby is proposing would see a four-per-cent-increase to the current top income tax bracket of $265,545 and higher.
That would mean, if re-elected, incomes of $190,504 to $265,545 and $265,545 to $1-million would be bumped up to 18.8 per cent and 22.5 per cent, respectively.
Anyone earning over $1 million annually would pay a 24.5 per cent tax rate on every dollar above that threshold.
According to the party, the changes would apply to less than four per cent of earners and only to income earned over each tax bracket.
The party also said Eby's proposed changes to would bring in an estimated $1 billion in revenue to "fund healthcare and lower costs."
"As we face an unprecedented attack on our economy and rising costs for working families, we’ll ask the wealthiest to chip in a little more," said Eby in a press release.

items: Confused by what's going on in B.C. politics? Catch up on the disarray

blocks.text: The leader made the announcement Sunday, while campaigning in Comox on Vancouver Island, after he toured ridings in southern British Columbia ahead of the Oct. 24 election day.

In response, the B.C. Conservatives said in a statement that the NDP plan would mean taxing the doctors and specialists every community is fighting to recruit, and would drive doctors out of the province.
"There is no problem the NDP don't think can be fixed by raising your taxes," the statement said.
The Conservatives have campaigned on a promise of never raising taxes.

B.C. Greens Leader Emily Lowan said taxing the incomes of B.C.'s most wealthy misses the point because most of the ultra-wealthy don't get rich on paychequaes. Rather, she said their fortunes grow in stocks and real estate. "His plan doesn't touch a cent of that," she said in a statement.

items: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby talks Trump, Conservatives and LNG ahead of Oct. 24 election

blocks.text: The New Democrats' proposal comes after Eby said his government would introduce price guards for certain groceries, as well as gasoline and diesel, while temporarily lowering the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents per litre.
