Eby said during the early phases of the campaign that his party would introduce a new tax on empty condominiums and lift the speculation and vacancy tax.
But Peter Milobar, B.C. Conservative Party candidate for Kamloops Centre, criticized the B.C. NDP leader Saturday for promises he made in the 2024 election that he says went unfulfilled.
He pointed to the 2024 campaign promise of giving families a rebate of $1,000 a year for groceries, before cancelling it in order to "find dollars" amid U.S. trade relations instability.
"These are serious times, and families need strong leadership, not a premier who treats promises like campaign props," said Milobar.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Polls close in Brazil as Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro remain neck and neck
articles.summary: If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.

blocks.text: Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race.
After casting his ballot, 80-year-old left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".
His challenger, right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".

The result is forecast to be close. BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that the gap between Lula and Bolsonaro is only two points. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.
According to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), more than 158.7 million Brazilians, including one million people abroad, are eligible to vote in the election.
Lula is challenged by 11 candidates, although BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that candidates other than Lula and Bolsonaro will get only about 10% of the vote.

The TSE has not set a fixed time for the release of the official results, but they are expected within hours because voting is electronic and experience from previous elections shows that results tend to come quickly.

A victory for Bolsonaro would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's re-election would create problems for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.
Some countries, from which Brazilians living overseas are able to vote, have already released preliminary vote count data.
In China, Lula won 56.63% of the votes, while Bolsonaro came in second with 31.33%. Lula also won in countries including South Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia.
In Israel, however, Bolsonaro won 74.40% of the valid votes. He also won 71.59% of the valid votes in Japan.
Today's result will also determine the composition of the Senate from February 2027 onwards, as 54 of the Senate's 81 seats are being contested, representing two-thirds of the chamber.
Currently, the largest bloc in the Senate is Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), followed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which has served in a coalition government under Lula.

In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father, Jair. But the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and is barred from standing for office.
Because of recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has been prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, there is little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has his father's backing.

articles.title: 'This is home for me': Amber Marshall reflects as 20th season of Heartland set to begin
articles.summary: Amber Marshall has grown up on Heartland, the long-running CBC drama that mirrors her real-life love of horses and ranch life. As the show celebrates its 20th season, its cast, characters and global…

image.caption: A young Amber Marshall learns how to ride a horse. (Submitted by Amber Marshall)

blocks.text: Heartland star Amber Marshall is an Alberta ranch girl in real life, too
For nearly 20 years, Amber Marshall has lived, in some ways, the life of Amy Fleming.
She was 19 when she began playing the horse-loving teenager at the centre of Heartland, the CBC drama about a family ranch in the Alberta Foothills.
Marshall has been riding since she was five, got her first horse at 10 and had long imagined a future surrounded by animals.
"I knew that that's who I wanted to be when I grew up," Marshall, now 38, told CBC's Ian Hanomansing in a new interview. "I wanted to be Amy Fleming."
Nearly two decades later, the distinction between actor and character has become unusually difficult to draw.
Marshall, who is from London, Ont., lives on a ranch of her own. She is surrounded by horses and cows, fosters dogs and has made Alberta her home. She moved there during Heartland’s second season.

items: Heartland's milestone 20th Season: Everything you need to know before the premiere on CBC Gem

blocks.text: "I can never see myself relocating again. This is home for me," she said.
Heartland, which begins its 20th season on Sunday, is the longest-running scripted drama in Canadian television history.

Based on the books by Lauren Brooke, it began airing in 2007 and has grown from a Canadian family series into an international phenomenon — with viewers in countries ranging from England and France to Australia and the United States.
The series follows Amy and her family as they work to keep their ranch operating while navigating growing up, relationships, grief and financial pressures.

Amy has married, become a mother and been widowed following the sudden death of her husband, Ty Borden (Graham Wardle). Her sister, Lou (Michelle Morgan), has built a career and raised a family, while their grandfather Jack (Shaun Johnston) has remained the family patriarch.
The characters have aged and changed, allowing viewers to grow up with them.

items: Heartland's youngest stars: The twins who play Lyndy grow up on the show

blocks.text: Marshall has met fans who were babies when the show began and have followed it through childhood and adolescence.
Some have told her that Heartland helped them through difficult periods in their lives.

"It’s special to know that a show can resonate with someone who's never been to Canada, that's never been to Alberta," she said, "and they can watch it and feel a connection to those characters and to that Heartland family."
A family story that resonates beyond Alberta
That connection was on display at a fan event in Alberta on Aug. 11, when viewers travelled from all over the globe.

Sarah Metcalf and her daughter, Riva, came from Manchester, England. Riva first encountered Heartland through a schoolbook when she was nine, then began watching the series after relatives in Canada sent the family DVDs.

"We watched one episode and it would leave on a cliffhanger, and then you'd have to watch the next one," Sarah said. "It’s a very special series, and we're very lucky that we came across it.... It’s a special part of us."

Leanne and Ayla Gale travelled from Brisbane, Australia. Ayla says the show’s performances and cinematography inspired her own interest in film, while her mother, Leanne, was drawn to the Alberta scenery. "I love Canada. I love the Rockies, the scenery, the mountains, pine trees, ranches,” Leanne said.
Marshall agrees that the landscape is central to the show. "The Heartland vista has become a character of its own," she said.
Fans often ask whether the Foothills are real or the product of green-screen effects. Marshall said they are and that the scenery has inspired some viewers to visit Alberta.
"It’s just a beautiful part of Canada," she said. "People want to feel and experience what they see on TV, and I don’t think they’re disappointed."

items: Heartland star Amber Marshall to guest star on Murdoch Mysteries

blocks.text: Marshall said visitors can experience the region’s western lifestyle, nature and "calming presence," becoming fully immersed in the Alberta Foothills.
She told Hanomansing that Alberta’s slower pace has taught her to resist the constant rush she notices when she returns to Ontario.
"I love being able to walk out in the field, say, 'You know what, I probably should be doing something else, but I'm just going to really enjoy this nice day,'" Marshall said.
Horses keep everyone present
That calm has shaped the Heartland set, where horses are central to the production. Marshall said their unpredictability keeps the series realistic and forces the actors to remain present.
"Horses are just living in the moment," she said. "They don't read the script, they don't know what's going on.”
The animals also require a quiet, relaxed workplace.
"You cannot have a tense set with animals and expect them to perform,” she said. "We have to be quiet. We have to be relaxed. We have to be calm."

Marshall's commitment to animals began long before Heartland. As a child, she wanted to become a veterinarian and volunteered at an animal shelter from the age of 10. She now runs the Foothills Animal Support Society, which helps animals and their families who might need access to veterinary care.
She has also spoken out against opening protected areas of the Rocky Mountains to coal mining, saying she has seen the damage caused to landscapes, water sources and animals.
"I do believe that we have a moral obligation to protect this beautiful place," she said.
'I'll do Heartland till I die'
Marshall said she believes Heartland endures because it offers something increasingly rare: wholesome, intergenerational television that leaves viewers feeling better instead of more anxious.
"It makes you feel very complete,” she said. "It makes you feel settled. It makes you feel like you've done something right for your mind and body."
She said the show is not confined to a particular era or stage of life. Its characters can continue to grow as new people arrive, others leave and families change.
As for how many seasons remain, her answer was immediate: "Oh gosh, another 20."
"I’ll do Heartland till I die," she said. "This is my life. I love being in Western Canada. I love being on a ranch. I love being surrounded by my animals."

articles.title: Nationalists top Bosnia-Herzegovina's divisive election
articles.summary: Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, the Serb nationalist candidate backed by disqualified secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, took the lead for the Serb seat of the three-member presidency in a vote with record-low…

image.caption: Preliminary results show strong results for ethnic-nationalist blocsImage: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bosnian officials reported a record-low turnout following the Sunday election, with only 41.5% out of the country's 3.4 million voters eligible to take part in the general election.
Polls closed in Bosnia-Herzegovina on Sunday evening, where around 3.4 million voters were eligible to take part in the Balkan country's general election.
With more than 90% of votes tallied, the Central Election Commission (CIK) said turnout for Sunday's election was a record-low 41.5%, down from 51.5% in 2022.
Nationalist parties dominated races as citizens chose officials across multiple tiers of government; including members of the country's multiethnic, tripartite presidency.

With counting nearly concluded, Serb nationalist Zeljka ​Cvijanovic, Bosniak moderate leftist Denis Becirovic and Croat nationalist ‌Darijana ​Filipovic have been announced as the winners of the presidential seats of their respective ethnicities.

Cvijanovic had been backed by the Republika Srpska's former secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik, who was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
"I am declaring that we have won," Dodik told supporters in Banja Luka on Sunday night. He said his SNSD party had retained the Serb seat in the presidency and remained power in Republika Srpska.

blocks.caption: Voters queued in Banja Luka and other cities around the countryImage: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: With counting nearly over, Cvijanovic looked to have won with 55.6% of the vote.
Social Democrat Becirovic won the race for the Bosniak seat with 38.1% of the vote, while Croat Filipovic took 48.2% of the vote.
Nationalist and ethnic political division

Voters also chose lawmakers for the federal parliament and the heads of institutions for the country's two largely autonomous entities — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and the Serb-run Republika Srpska (RS).
Currently, about 50% of Bosnia and Herzegovina's citizens are Muslim Bosniaks, 31% are Orthodox Serb and another 15% are Catholic Croat.

Between 1992 and 1995, more than two milion people were displaced and nearly 100,000 killed in a civil war started by Serbia. The country has been peaceful in recent years but ethnonationalist parties have kept divisions alive even as voters say they want to move on from the war-era rhetoric.
The election comes at a time when the country is struggling with a number of challenges.

There's been an economic downturn, sluggish progress toward EU membership, and sustained political gridlock — with dominant ethnic parties from these entities repeatedly stalling decisions by the weak central government that binds them.
The election saw contests that pitted the Bosniak ​SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party.

Polls closed at 7 p.m. local time (1700 GMT), with preliminary results to be released later in the evening — though complex constitutional order and drawn out coalition talks mean that the true result of Sunday's election could remain unclear for months.
What is the system that governs Bosnia-Herzegovina?

The economic, administrative and political responsibilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are divided between the multiethnic central government, the two semi-autonomous entities FBiH and RS, and the self-governing neutral Brcko district.
These entities are further split into several cantons and communities.

The complicated framework — divided along ethnic lines — was set up during the US-brokered 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, following the 1992-95 Bosnian war, itself a consequence of the breakup of Yugoslavia.
Milorad Dodik not on the ballot but still dominant in Republika Srpska
In Republika Srpska, secessionist leader ​Milorad Dodik of the SNSD party remained the key figure of the election despite not being on the ballot.

Dodik, the former president of the Serb-majority entity, is barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
Dodik-backed Savo Minic decisively won the Republika Srpska's presidency and RS increased its heft by taking 39% of the parliamentary tally, up from 34.6% in 2022.
Dodik, who just returned from meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, wants close ‌ties to Serbia and Russia and seccession from Bosnia and Herzegovina.
"Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead, it is an impossible country," Dodik told supporters at the final rally of his in Banja Luka on Friday.
What is happening in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
In the Muslim-Croat federation, Bosniak parties are advocating for a stronger central state.
The main Bosniak SDA party is focused on efforts to keep the country united against Serb separatism.
Bosnian Croats are also largely backing their ethnic parties, including the Bosnian branch of Croatia's ruling conservative Croatian Democratic Union.
Meanwhile, Denis Becirovic, the incumbent Bosniak presidency member, has vowed a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
EU ambitions
Bosnia and Herzegovina has been a candidate for EU membership since 2022.
But the actual start of membership talks depends on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, including strengthening judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption ​laws.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028

articles.title: Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results
articles.summary:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential race

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son…

blocks.text: The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. The president in Brazil is directly elected, and candidates need more than 50% of the vote to avoid a second round. Polls close at 17.00 BRT / 21.00 BST.
Live first round results
Guardian graphic. Source: TES
How the election works

Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.

According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.

Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars.

Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.

Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.

One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.
Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

articles.title: Pakistan: Imran Khan supporters demand ex-PM's release
articles.summary: Thousands of Imran Khan supporters have begun a trek to Islamabad to demand he be freed as Pakistan's political leadership remains in deadlock. The government has set up roadblocks to keep protesters…

image.caption: Imran Khan's supporters hope to inspire hundreds of thousands of Pakistanis to get behind the ex-PM's cause Image: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of Imran Khan supporters began to make their way to the Pakistani capital Islamabad on Sunday as a slow moving convoy set off on an 80-kilometer (50-mile) trip that will take several days to complete.
Some 5,000 supporters are traveling by bus, car and truck from northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party (PTI) holds power.

March organizers say they intend to rally hundreds of thousands of supporters to Khan's cause along the way, hoping to bring about his release from prison as well as his transfer to a hospital where he can receive medical treatment and regular visits from his family.
Government officials say Khan is in no need of hospitalization and that he receives regular visits already.
In August, Pakistan's Supreme Court ruled that he should be moved to a civilian hospital but authorities returned him to prison after a short stay at a government-run medical facility.

blocks.caption: Several rallies will be held along the journey to IslamabadImage: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Imran Khan still very influential despite being behind bars for years

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence inside Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.

Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, left office in April 2022, when he lost a no-confidence vote. He has been in prison since August 2023. Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023.
Moreover, his supporters say the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Speaking with AFP news agency, James Dorsey of the National University of Singapore called Khan "a populist leader" with "a genuine popular movement that has broad popular support," adding, "That's why I think you've seen the determination by the government to prevent (protesters) from entering Islamabad."

Dorsey noted that in his opinion, security concerns — particularly those stemming from Pakistan's unresolved February 2026 war with Afghanistan — would likely force Islamabad to avoid escalation in the face of protests.
The march, he says, is "a problem for the government, but I don't think it's an existential threat."

blocks.caption: Organizers say the march will grow from 5,000 supporters as they advance toward Islamabad this week  Image: Maaz Awan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan's government accuses Khan supporters of having terrorist sympathies

The march was initially set to commence on September 27, but organizers postponed it amid talks aimed at finding a political solution to the standoff between the government of Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif and Imran Khan's PTI — and despite the government erecting massive roadblocks in and around Islamabad.
The march began after those talks failed.
PTI Chairman Gohar Khan on Sunday said negotiations to stave off the march had remained deadlocked after two rounds of talks.
Khan's supporters now plan to hold rallies at a series of overnight stops during what will likely be a four or five day march.

Speaking from atop a large truck, the trailer of which is emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi said the movement will bring Pakistan's political standoff to the heart of the capital.
Why Pakistan is fighting the Taliban it once backed
Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the breakdown in negotiations, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the march.
In the past, protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including in 2024, when security personnel and civilians were killed.
Pakistan has also seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government cited these as reason for delaying the march.

The government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks. The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

articles.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
articles.summary: An Anthropic report says the AI model Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in the Central African Republic. Similar allegations were raised for the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Sudan…

image.caption: The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agentsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled "Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.

The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.
Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition

The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

blocks.caption: According to Anthropic, Russia is using AI in African countries to spread its messagesImage: Fred de Noyelle/Godong/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW. "They’ve been doing this for several years now."Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.

"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.

Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.
'The government wants to get rid of us,' opposition says

For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW.

"There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."

blocks.caption: An arial view of Bangui, Central African RepublicImage: Sam Mednick/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."
AI influence operations across the DRC, Kenya, Sudan and Mali?

Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya, Sudan and Mali were also affected.

In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.
In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.

blocks.caption: Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario AmodeiImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.

In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.
Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
articles.summary: Pike's lawyer says doctors are still trying to clear two lethal doses of pentobarbital from her body.

blocks.text: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.
Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.
Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."
He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.
He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.

Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday.

"If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."

He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement."
"We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.
She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges.
Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful.
"I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.
The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".

Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

articles.title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
articles.summary: The allegations were made after police detained dozens of protesters demanding the resignation of the election chief over changes to voter rolls.

blocks.text: Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.
The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.
In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".
"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.
She said the police were resorting to "brutality".

articles.title: ICC amends e-court protocol ahead of Duterte trial
articles.summary: Less than two months before the start of the crimes against humanity trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has amended its protocol for digital evidence…

blocks.text: October 5, 2026 | 12:00am
The International Criminal Court is investigating killings linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte's anti-drug campaign, which rights groups say left thousands dead.
Philstar.com / illustration

MANILA, Philippines — Less than two months before the start of the crimes against humanity trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has amended its protocol for digital evidence and other information on witnesses and victims.
The ICC Registry, which is in charge of the administrative aspects of the court, submitted last week the amended E-Court Protocol that will be used during Duterte’s trial.

“This Protocol defines the standards according to which the participants should prepare and provide evidence, potential evidence and material in electronic form with the Court,” read the document submitted to the ICC Trial Chamber III.

“Furthermore, this Protocol defines metadata which should accompany the materials submitted. These standards are designed to minimize the document management and technology costs to the participants and the Court and to allow for the efficient management of proceedings,” it added.

Trial judges earlier directed the ICC Registry to submit the amended E-Court Protocol after it granted the prosecution’s request to add a URL (uniform resource locator) metadata field for each of the open source or user-generated evidence submitted in the case.
The prosecution said the additional field will allow parties to easily identify the URL or link “associated with the open source evidence at the time it was captured.”
The judges, however, denied the defense’s request for an additional “expert verification” field to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence.

“The (defense’s) requested amendment, if implemented, requires the Prosecution to prepare additional materials that contain information regarding the relevance and admissibility of open-source and user-generated evidence, before the Defense analyses evidence and raises any abovementioned issues,” read the Sept. 26 decision.
Defense lawyer Peter Haynes argued that there is a need for extra caution to ensure that evidence is properly verified before it is submitted to the court.
But the ICC prosecutor said adding a separate expert verification field is “unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency.”

articles.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
articles.summary:
Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged while whereabouts of other five remain unknown

An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days…

blocks.text: An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

blocks.caption: Egyptian authorities have charged the journalist Mohamed Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading fake news. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP

blocks.text: Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human-rights record, but has largely kept the majority of funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, read a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsada2sh are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

articles.title: Yemen announces military campaign to reclaim land from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.summary: The Yemeni president's announcement comes amid an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.

blocks.text: But it is not yet clear whether this represents a new phase in the conflict.
The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis are engaged in a fierce battle with government forces for control of the region, as they seek to secure coastal areas and, by extension, the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.
Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.
Away from Yemen, the Houthis are also trying to hurt the Saudis with an attack aimed at the country's economic lifeblood - oil.

On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."

It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".
But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.
In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.
On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.
Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.
After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.
The Houthis have launched a blockade of Saudi energy exports, which have already been squeezed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Would slashing migration tank the economy or reset Australia’s living standards? Canada may offer clues
articles.summary:
Annual population growth for the North American nation has slowed to just 0.5% – and the economy is ‘adjusting’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Would slashing net overseas migration “trash the economy” or deliver the necessary population “reset” to restore Australia’s stagnant living standards?
Labor and an ascendant One Nation have presented starkly different visions of what a migration program in the national interest looks like.

Pauline Hanson, the populist party’s leader, last month announced a plan to cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years by targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.
To achieve that reduction, net overseas migration (Nom) would need to turn negative for three years, the party says, before an ongoing cap of 130,000.
That compares with Labor’s longer-term Nom target of 225,000, and to the last official estimate of 292,000 in the year to March.
Tony Burke, the home affairs minister, said One Nation’s plan, if enacted, would “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”.
Hanson disagrees, and is quick to blame Australia’s high population growth over the past few years for the economy’s woes.
In a social media post, she said “vested interest [sic] are warning Australia could face a technical recession if migration is cut”.
“Australians have been in a per-capita recession for years. Their lives have been getting worse because of migration. Canada has shown living standards improve when migration is cut.”
For those looking for international comparisons, Canada has long been a type of sister country to Australia – similar size, similar culture, similar economy.
And the North American nation is in the midst of a dramatic migration adjustment that has flattened population growth.

Unlike Hanson, Canada’s policymakers have not targeted a specific net overseas migration level. Instead, they have rolled out a suite of policies to reduce the number of temporary migrants as a share of population from a peak of 7.6% in 2024, to 5%.

Canada is about halfway to this goal. The government has done this by reducing temporary arrivals, particularly international students, making it harder to extend stays, and giving some temporary migrants permanency.
Annual population growth has slowed from 3.1% in early 2024 to just 0.5% now.
So how well has Canada’s economy coped? And what does their experience tell us about how Australia should respond to growing calls for a more hardline approach to migration?
‘Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting’
In May, the CD Howe Institute, a leading Canadian thinktank, issued a report on the country’s economy in a “lower immigration era”.
The title was “resetting expectations”.
Modelling by the report’s authors, Don Drummond and Parisa Mahboubi, estimated that employment in Canada could fall this year and the next.
Real GDP growth in 2026 may be no more than 0.5%, they forecast, and “little more” than 1% on average in the long term.
Falling employment would normally be cause for alarm, but Drummond and Mahboubi say this is actually “what a normally operating labour market delivers, given the demographic shifts underway”.
“These are not signs of a struggling economy,” they said.
“Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting. Understanding that adjustment is a precondition for sound policy in the years ahead.”

blocks.caption: The Canadian economy has been ‘relatively resilient’, experts say. Pictured: Vancouver Photograph: Charles Mistral/Alamy

blocks.text: Nathan Janzen, the assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, agrees with this assessment.
“What the population shifts have done has changed how we need to interpret economic data.”

The university sector has been hit particularly hard by the tighter migration rules. The government also provided exceptions to migrants working in areas of particular labour shortages, such as agriculture and the care economy.
But overall, Janzen says, “the Canadian economy has been relatively resilient”.
“If our population estimate numbers are right, we could have negative employment growth and still have falling unemployment. And the per capita economy looks like it’s getting better.”
after newsletter promotion
Canada’s recession and ‘cyclical factors’ at play
But economists warn against assuming Canada’s experience would be replicated here.
Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, says the first point to make is that Canada’s post-pandemic surge was far larger than Australia’s.
“While people here get excited about our post-Covid immigration, it was nothing compared to theirs,” Kearns says.
Even now, Canada’s population still sits 5% above where it would have been expected to be based on pre-Covid trends.
In comparison, Australia’s population is tracking just 0.2% above its pre-pandemic trend line.
“So the decline [in Canada’s population growth] has to be taken in context of the massive run-up,” Kearns says.
Canada also began its migration crackdown at a time of high unemployment in the wake of an aggressive series of interest rate hikes by the Bank of Canada.
In contrast, were Australia to crack down hard on migrants, it would do so with a tight labour market where unemployment sits at 4.6% and at a time of widespread labour shortages.
Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, says: “I don’t think you can just point to Canada and say, ‘Look, they did OK.’”
Ellis says there are cyclical factors at play that help explain Canada’s apparent economic resilience to its migration crackdown.
“It’s also because they are recovering from a recession,” she says.
The challenge of ageing populations
While Canada’s economy has, so far, coped with the country’s stricter migration policies, there is little appetite for them to be a permanent feature in a nation that remains open to immigration.
Canada, like Australia, is ageing. That means a shrinking share of taxpaying workers to fund the cost of providing pensions, aged care and health services to older Canadians.

The CD Howe Institute analysis shows that if the current era of low population growth became a permanent one, then Canada’s economy would be about 11.5% smaller by 2060, compared with official government projections.
“The implications for fiscal sustainability are significant,” the authors said. “This gap translates into structurally weaker revenues and higher debt ratios.”
Janzen says that, without immigration, “labour shortages are going to be a structural feature of the economy”.
“The view is that this will be a temporary adjustment, before we return to something more like historical rates of immigration.”

And while Australia may not want to exactly replicate our North American peer’s dramatic migration reset, there remain legitimate questions around how we can better manage a temporary migration program that has ballooned over recent years.

Ellis believes Australian employers have become too reliant on overseas labour, from chefs to workers in rural areas, and that this has come at the expense of training and hiring locals, even if it means paying higher wages.

“By choosing higher population growth with a high temporary component, we have made it easy for employers to look offshore any time they need to find someone for a job. There are definitely industries that have grown to be reliant on that,” she says.
“That degrades your ability and willingness to train your local workforce.”

items: Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor

articles.title: US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say
articles.summary:
Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’

A US marine stationed on

blocks.text: A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.

US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.

The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.

“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

articles.title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar
articles.summary:
Calyton said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but it also posed ‘a threat’ during his DNI Senate confirmation hearing

Donald Trump on Sunday named

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to serve also as the new White House AI czar.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
During his Senate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger”, but it also posed “a threat”.
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.
CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.

Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.

In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans.
The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.
Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.

But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – who he previously promised would be led by a “High IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.

On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.
Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.

David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.
Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton is ‘“a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

articles.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.summary: Two residents in Mekelle tell the BBC pro-government forces have taken control of the city.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on Sunday
ByTeklemariam Bekiteditor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack Burgess
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.

Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.

Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

blocks.caption: BBC map of Ethiopia showing the northern states of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The regional capital of Mekelle is labelled in Tigray and the national capital Addis Ababa is also located near the centre of the country and just outside the three northern states. Eritrea is shown to the north, borderin…

blocks.text: On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.

Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.

The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Kyiv bridge hit in further drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
articles.summary: Unverified video shows a drone hitting the Northern Bridge as vehicles move across it.

blocks.text: A major bridge in Kyiv has been targeted by Russian strikes for the second day in a row, coinciding with a surprise visit from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's to the city.
The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was hit on Sunday morning, a day after it was first struck by drones in an attack that damaged the road surface and led to traffic disruption.
Kyiv Major Vitali Klitschko said Sunday's strike had also damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.
Major bridges have been targeted in Kyiv over the past four days as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the capital.

Unverified video footage of Sunday's strike shows cars moving on the bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.
Klitschko reported the strike on Telegram, writing: "Hitting the roadway on the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way to the scene."
As emergency services responded to the incident, Germany's Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine and pledged further assistance to bolster Ukrainian air defences.
He wrote on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.
"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."

articles.title: Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia strikes bridge
articles.summary: A Kyiv bridge was hit by a Russian drone shortly after Chancellor Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital. During his visit, Merz is set to announce new measures to support Ukraine, including plans for…

image.caption: Friedrich Merz joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in paying tribute to fallen Ukrainian soldiersImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday morning, accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading German economic figures.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon his arrival by train.
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.

During his visit, Merz is expected to announce a new raft of measures to support Ukraine in its fight against the ongoing Russian invasion, including a further billion euros in German military aid, plus €350 million ($395 million) for energy sector repairs, according to German media reports.
The chancellor is also expected to unveil plans for the co-production of interceptor drones and long-range missiles both in Ukraine and Germany.

blocks.caption: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv by train on Sunday morningImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Focus on ramping up drone production

According to German government sources cited by the Reuters and dpa news agencies, arms production is expected to focus on the development and delivery of thousands of drones capable of intercepting the rapid, jet-powered drones increasingly being deployed by the Russian military against civilian infrastructure targets in Ukraine.

The production of missiles with a range of over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) is also expected to be ramped up, enhancing Ukraine's ability to strike military and logistical targets far beyond the frontline and inside Russia itself.
Merz is expected to emphasize how Germany also stands to benefit from the expanded cooperation, both in terms of its own defense against Russian hybrid activities and in terms of jobs and technology.
The chancellor is also expected to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the progress of political reforms in Ukraine and the continuing battle against corruption.
Can Ukraine still count on Germany?
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge during Merz visit
The visit comes just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.

"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."

In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
Another strike followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation has not been deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Russia targets Kyiv bridge network
Merz: 'If Germany wavers, Ukraine wavers'
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.

His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.

"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."

Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin.
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.

articles.title: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Shadow justice secretary says despite U-turn Labour are still ‘restricting juries by the back door’, as Conservative conference begins in Birmingham

Good morning. Anthony…

blocks.text: Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials

Good morning. Anthony Seldon recently published the latest in his long and invaluable series of inside stories of premierships, Sunak at 10, and he gave it the subtitle “The last Conservative prime minister?” When the book was being planned in the early days of Kemi Badenoch’s leadership of the Conservative party, it did look as though the Tories might be finished as a party of government. But now Seldon, and his co-author Tom Egerton, aren’t so sure. Their book concludes: “At the time of writing in July 2026 … the Tory party still needs to engage in a process of deep self-reflection to understand why it failed in government, and tore itself so destructively apart, if it is ever to regain power. But at this point in time we believe it is unlikely that Sunak will have been the last Tory prime minister.”

That is a victory, of sorts, for Badenoch. For most of last year there were doubts that she would still be leader by the time of the next election. But she gave a successful party conference speech, her response to the budget was much admired, and her personal approval ratings with Tory members and right-leaning voters shot up. After two years as opposition leader, Iain Duncan Smith was booted out. Two years in, Badenoch’s position as leader is safe and it is even conceivable that she could stay on if the Conservatives were to lose the next election (in part because any Tories who favour a radically different policy approach are being purged from the candidates list).

But that does not mean Badenoch’s leadership is going well. At the last election the Conservatives won 24.4% of the GB vote. According to the Politico poll of polls, they have been consistently polling below that since the end of 2024 and they are currently on 19%.

The Conservative conference starts today and, explaining her strategy in an interview in the Times, Badenoch said: “Last year was about telling the party who I was. Now the party is going to be showing the country who we are: a strong team of people who actually like each other.” The Tories have already announced quite a lot of conference-related policy.

But she has not got the news space all to herself. It is the final day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton and this morning activists are expected to debate their ‘Zionism is racism’ motion. The proposal has split the party, and critics claim that it is antisemitic. Whatever happens, it will affect how the Green party is seen.
And this morning Labour has announced a major U-turn – abandoning most of the Keir Starmer/David Lammy plans to restrict access to jury trials. Haroon Siddique has the story here.

In the past, there was an unofficial ‘gentleman’s agreement’ that the government did not make big news announcements during the opposition party’s conference. But that era (like two-party politics) is over, and Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has successfully kept Badenoch off the top of this morning’s news cycle.
Still, the Tories can claim this as a victory. This is from Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.

double quotation markThis is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour has been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the crown court.
But Timothy also claimed the U-turn did not go far enough.

double quotation markLabour are restricting juries by the back door, scrapping the right to elect one and dumping those cases on magistrates whose backlog is at a record high. Nearly 81,000 cases are stuck in the crown court, yet there is no commitment to get courts sitting more often, but Labour did find the time to write into law a review of how its reforms treat people of different backgrounds.
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, is interviewed on Sky’s Sunday with Helen Lewis.
9am: Kemi Badenoch is interviewed on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. (The interview has been pre-recorded.) Norris is being interviewed too.
Morning: The Green party debates the controversial ‘Zionism is racism’ motion on the final day of its conference this morning.

2pm: John Belsley, president of the National Conservative Convention, opens the proceedings at the Tory conference in Birmingham. The session is on the theme of “resisting separatism” and the speakers include Alex Burghart, the deputy leader and shadow Northern Ireland secretary; Mims Davies, shadow Welsh secretary; Harriet Cross, shadow Scottish secretary; Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd; and Russell Findlay, the Scottish leader.
Mid afternoon: Badenoch delivers her opening speech to the conference.
4pm: James Cleverly, who wants to be the Tory candidate for London mayor in 2028, is speaking at a fringe event.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
articles.summary:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China…

blocks.text: Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.

EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.

Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.

“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.

“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.

Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.

The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion

Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”

Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”

He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title: Rare tornado whips through small Australian town
articles.summary: The twister was caught on camera in Ulladulla, New South Wales, damaging property and downing trees.
